power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Food odours are often used to study anticipatory food reward, yet it remains unclear whether they evoke stronger reward responses than other odours or food cues presented in other sensory modalities.
We systematically reviewed the literature to evaluate these assumptions.
Methods: MEDLINE, Embase and Web of Science were searched.
Experimental studies investigating behavioural reward responses to orthonasal food odours in healthy participants were included.
Two primary contrasts were considered: (1) food vs. non-food odours and (2) food odours vs. food stimuli, as well as the influence of hunger and satiety.
Risk of bias was assessed using QualSyst and certainty of evidence using GRADE.
A co-occurrence network of odours used in the field was constructed.
Results: Of the 64 included studies, 11 compared food with non-food odours (total N = 363) statistically, while three compared food odours with pictures (total N = 216).
Evidence for greater reward responses to food than non-food odours was limited and inconsistent, although positive findings tended to originate from larger studies.
Evidence suggesting that food pictures elicit stronger reward responses than food odours was limited due to the small evidence base and methodological heterogeneity.
Across studies, odour selection was concentrated on a small number of stimuli.
Conclusions: Few studies have directly examined assumptions underlying the use of food odours as reward stimuli.
Greater methodological standardisation and explicit stimulus comparisons are needed to establish under which experimental conditions food odours provide an optimal model of anticipatory food reward.

text.text: Accordingly, research on food perception or eating behaviour draws on a wide range of stimulus materials, including real foods, images, odours (both orthonasal and retronasal), tastes, and flavours.

Likewise, outcomes of interest might cover basic assessments of hedonic features of the stimulus material, intent to buy or consume, the amount consumed, or more abstract concepts like approach/avoidance or parameters estimated from decision-making paradigms.

This methodological flexibility presents a challenge to those interested in researching eating behaviours through sensory perception: stimulus choices are not neutral, but can shape the resulting behavioural and hedonic responses, and the sensory modality by which the stimulus is delivered represents one key source of this variation.
A further source of variation in behavioural outcomes stems from the context in which a study is conducted.

The perception of food stimuli is dependent on both external factors, such as the research environment, and internal influences, such as the participant's current metabolic state (hunger vs. satiety).

For example, in the framework of sensory-specific satiety (SSS), foods will be liked less after having been eaten to satiety than they were before, while non-eaten foods retain their original pleasantness (Rolls et al., 1981).

Since both orthonasal food odours and pictures function as predictive cues for</ref> food before consumption, both can be well suited to studying reward processes.

text.text: During the food reward processing cycle, the smell or sight of food triggers an appetitive response that drives approach behaviour.

text.text: Unlike visual food cues, which primarily represent a future eating experience, orthonasal odours may simultaneously function as predictive cues and as sensory experiences in their own right.
Consequently, responses to food odours may reflect both the experienced pleasantness of the odour itself and reward processes associated with anticipated consumption.

Despite the multisensory nature of food perception, relatively few studies have directly compared the effectiveness of different stimulus modalities or systematically examined the use of specific stimulus categories.
To date, the majority of studies on eating behaviour and food choice employ only visual stimuli as food cues, which are more easily administered compared to olfactory cues.

Howeverhttps://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=2018117&pre=&suf=&sa=0&dbf=0 the dual nature of olfactory perception through orthonasal and retronasal routes, as well as its direct connection to pathways that bypass thalamic processing (Seubert et al., 2013) , may confer unique advantages to investigations of the different reward components.

text.text: Given these considerations, two key questions arise.
First, whether it can be established experimentally that food-associated odours reliably carry higher hedonic value than non-food odours that are less linked to a specific motivational drive.
Second, whether food odour stimulation is a more effective tool to evoke hedonic and motivational responses to food than other sensory modalities, such as visual representations of food.

These questions were operationalised in the current review through two main comparisons: (1) reward responses to food vs. non-food odours (i.e., differences in object category associations) (2) reward responses to food stimuli presented in the olfactory domain compared to other sensory modalities (i.e., differences in sensory modality).
Across both comparisons, we examined the role of metabolic state (e.g., hunger vs. satiety) as a motivational factor and potential moderator of these effects.

To contextualise any observed differences in hedonic value, we further examined the range and frequency of odour stimuli used across studies, allowing us to assess the generalisability of findings within the field.

By identifying whether and how food and non-food odours differ in their hedonic value, as well as how they compare to other sensory modalities, this review maps the hedonic landscape of food-related stimuli across modalities.
In doing so, it provides a foundation for more informed methodological choices in experimental studies of eating behaviour.

text.text: Studies were considered for inclusion in this review if they had an experimental design and examined the reward of orthonasal (non-)food odours and other food stimuli (e.g., pictures/symbols/other) in healthy subjects, including those with a healthy control group.
We concentrated on studies that used behavioural outcome measures, such as reported ratings of hedonics, intent to consume, or willingness to pay.

Studies that were excluded included animal studies, those involving children too young to indicate behavioural preferences (i.e., newborns, infants, or toddlers), neuroimaging studies without behavioural outcomes, cell/in-vitro studies, studies that did not involve food odours, studies related to aromatherapy, and studies on product development.

Each title and abstract was independently reviewed for inclusion by two reviewers using Rayyan (Ouzzani et al., 2016) and, in case of disagreement, at least three authors discussed until agreement was reached.

text.text: Synthesis of results was based on the direction and statistical significance of the reported comparisons of interest (food vs. non-food odours; food odours vs. other sensory modalities), together with qualitative summaries of the reported findings.
Where applicable, the direction of the reported effect (Figure 4A) and a network representation of odour co-occurrences across studies were additionally visualised.

text.text: Potential sources of heterogeneity were explored qualitatively by comparing study characteristics, including participant populations, experimental design, stimulus selection, reward measures, and hunger or satiety manipulations.
No sensitivity analyses were conducted because no quantitative synthesis or meta-analysis was performed.
To create an overview of stimuli used across included studies, odours were labelled based on their reported perceptual quality.

Perceptual descriptors were taken directly from the original publications where available; when chemical compounds were listed without odour qualities, these were inferred from reference databases (e.g., Good Scents Company) and marked with an asterisk (*, see Supplementary Material 3).

Where multiple papers referred to the same or highly similar odour using different descriptors (e.g., "shampoo" vs. "classical shampoo fragrance"), these were standardised into a single label to streamline analysis.
Proprietary odours without available sensory descriptions were retained under their reported names (e.g., "Lovely ion" by EmoSens).
Next, perceptual descriptors were standardised across studies to reflect primary stimulus identity (e.g.
"Almond" and "Almond/marzipan" retaining the same label).
Where composite labels, such as "sweet rose" or "cleaning product (rosemary)", were reported, descriptors were simplified to the core odour to enable aggregation across studies.

All perceptual odour labels were then grouped into classes of perceptual similarity (e.g., rose and lilac receiving the class name "floral"): Chemical/synthetic/medicinal, dairy/fatty, environmental, floral, fruity, herbs/spices, savoury/meaty, sour/pungent, sweet or woody/green plant.

Proprietary or scene-based odours lacking identifiable perceptual descriptors were retained but grouped into "Unclassified", reflecting the absence of a definable odour category rather than perceptual similarity.

The complete set of stimuli was then filtered to only include studies that statistically analysed at least one contrast of interest; either comparing food and non-food odours or comparing food odours to stimuli from another modality.

text.text: The checklist for quality assessment of individual studies addresses potential issues such as blinding, randomisation, and sample size using a total of 14 items.
For each included study, two independent raters (LS and PAK) decided whether the criteria were met ("yes" = 2, "partial" = 1, "no" = 0, "N/A" = not applicable).
The raters then compared ratings and discussed any discrepancies for each item until agreement was reached before calculating a final score (ranging from 0 to 1) for each paper.
Notably, risk of bias was only calculated for those papers whose main study outcome was one of the contrasts of interest.

Studies that assessed liking for odours representing edible and non-edible objects, but did not explicitly compare these two categories statistically, were included in this review but not evaluated using the risk of bias tool.

text.text: Here, we evaluated this domain using the QualSyst (see above).
(2) Inconsistency of results across studies is examined by assessing the variability in effect estimates.
(3) Indirectness assesses the applicability of the evidence to the research question, considering whether the populations, interventions, comparators, and outcomes studied are directly relevant.
(4) Imprecision of the results focusing on the uncertainty of effect estimates due to factors such as sample size and the width of confidence intervals.

(5) Publication bias involves investigating whether the studies included in the review are representative of the entire evidence base or if there is selective publication of studies with positive results.
This domain was used to assess the risk of bias due to missing results (reporting bias) qualitatively.

The study design determined the initial rating of the evidence quality, with randomised controlled trials typically starting as "high-quality evidence" and observational studies as "lowquality evidence".
The quality of evidence can then be downgraded based on issues identified in the domains or upgraded if certain factors, such as a large magnitude of effect, increase confidence in the results.
In an effort to adapt GRADE to non-clinical research, we started the assessment with "high-quality evidence", since all included papers presented experimental research.
In applying the GRADE system to this review, we then carefully evaluated the body of evidence for each research question.
The final quality ratings were then summarised and used to guide the strength of conclusions drawn from the review, ensuring that our evaluation of the evidence is systematic and reliable.
The first and second searches resulted in 15,916 and 1,906 studies respectively, and the citation search of included studies added 1,163 papers.
After deduplication and screening of abstracts and full texts, a total of 64 papers were included in this review.

Overall, the evidence does not establish a consistent preference for food over non-food odours, with observed differences potentially depending on metabolic state, participant characteristics and stimulus selection.

The interpretability of findings across studies is further limited by several methodological factors, such as uneven stimulus set sizes for food vs. non-food (Piacentini et al., 1993) or the inclusion of food-related odours (e.g., coffee) within the non-food stimulus set (Goldzak-Kunik et al., 2012).

text.text: Eating behaviour is inherently a multisensory process, where reward-related information from different senses contributes to decisions about whether and what to eat.
Consequently, researchers aiming to study food reward in laboratory settings are faced with the challenge of selecting appropriate methods and sensory stimuli to capture these processes.

The present review, therefore, aimed to examine two related questions: whether food odours are associated with greater hedonic value than non-food odours, and how food odours compare to food stimuli presented in other sensory modalities.

text.text: Of note, these odours were found in up to 30 studies, while most other odours were much less common.

Studies that statistically addressed one of our contrasts of interest likewise demonstrated that a handful of olfactory stimuli (i.e. chocolate, strawberry, bacon, lavender, rose) occurred and co-occurred across research, thereby potentially limiting the generalisability of outcomes.

Depending on whether or not researchers want their stimulus material to be easily recognisable to participants, the odour index presented here could facilitate the selection of stimuli for future studies that could incorporate the less commonly used materials.
The literature search uncovered a total of 64 studies, which assessed the rewarding properties of food and non-food odours, mainly through self-reported ratings.
However, of those, 50 did not statistically compare the two stimulus categories of interest.

text.text: Surprisingly, however, this assumption has received relatively little direct empirical attention.
This review identified 11 studies that investigated differences in the rewarding properties of food and non-food odours.
This contrast had low certainty of evidence, mainly due to inconsistency and imprecision in the findings.

text.text: We also observe that metabolic state influenced motivational responses towards food cues.
However, the inconsistent implementations of such manipulations likely further contributed to the variability in outcomes.
Across studies, hunger and satiety frequently moderated reward responses, although the observed effects were not entirely consistent.

There was some evidence that satiety primarily reduced responses to food odours, resulting in decreases in liking and wanting, while https://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=3618121,3136285&pre=&pre=&suf=&suf=&sa=0,0&dbf=0&dbf=0  (Albrecht et al., 2009; Plailly et al., 2011) https://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=3618121,3136285&pre=&pre=&suf=&suf=&sa=0,0&dbf=0&dbf=0 reward value of food-related cues changes in accordance with current physiological needs (Cabanac, 1971).

Such findings align with the concept of alliesthesia, whereby the</ref> reward value of food-related cues changes in accordance with current physiological needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cabanac, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: However, these effects did not appear to be uniform across all food stimuli.

In some of the reviewed studies, changes in reward responses varied as a function of food https://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=3136285,3771838&pre=&pre=&suf=&suf=&sa=0,0&dbf=0&dbf=0  (Plailly et al., 2011; Soussignan et al., 2012) https://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=3136285,3771838&pre=&pre=&suf=&suf=&sa=0,0&dbf=0&dbf=0 may not be specific to food odours and instead reflect broader changes in hedonic sensitivity (Piacentini et al., 1993).

text.text: Collectively, these findings suggest that hunger does not exert a simple uniform effect on food odour reward but rather interacts with characteristics of both the stimuli and the experimental design.

Studies differed with respect to fasting duration (ranging from a couple of hours to overnight fasts), meal composition, whether food intake was standardised, ad libitum or participants' own meals, within-vs. between-subject designs and counterbalancing procedures.

In several cases, hunger and satiety conditions were additionally confounded with time of day, with https://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=3136285,3771838,1519006,13640120&pre=&pre=&pre=&pre=&suf=&suf=&suf=&suf=&sa=0,0,0,0&dbf=0&dbf=0&dbf=0&dbf=0  (Fontana et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2015; Plailly et al., 2011; Soussignan et al., 2012) https://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=3136285,3771838,1519006,13640120&pre=&pre=&pre=&pre=&suf=&suf=&suf=&suf=&sa=0,0,0,0&dbf=0&dbf=0&dbf=0&dbf=0 difficult to disentangle from metabolic effects.

text.text: An additional consideration concerns the specificity of the experimentally induced satiety, as evidence from sensory-specific satiety suggests that reward decreases primarily for foods that have just been consumed, whereas uneaten foods retain much of their original hedonic value (Cabanac, 1971; Rolls et al., 1981).
text.formatted: An additional consideration concerns the specificity of the experimentally induced satiety, as evidence from sensory-specific satiety suggests that reward decreases primarily for foods that have just been consumed, whereas uneaten foods retain much of their original hedonic value <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cabanac, 1971;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Rolls et al., 1981)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the impact of a satiety manipulation also depends on the relationship between the consumed meal and the presented odours.
Accordingly, we propose that meal composition be matched to the presented odours or deliberately varied by including both matching and non-matching odours to directly investigate these effects.

Taken together, the available evidence suggests that food odours can, under certain circumstances, elicit stronger reward responses than non-food odours, but these differences are not universally observed.

Rather than reflecting contradictory evidence, much of the variability may stem from differences in statistical power, stimulus selection, and particularly from heterogeneous implementations of hunger and satiety manipulations.

Future studies would therefore benefit from more standardised metabolic-state protocols that explicitly consider fasting duration, meal composition, sensory-specific satiety, counterbalancing, and time-of-day effects.

text.text: Given the multisensory nature of eating, it is surprising how little evidence exists to guide researchers in selecting the most appropriate sensory modality to study anticipatory food reward.
The evidence discussed here has been inconsistent, imprecise, and subject to potential publication bias, and consequently graded to be of very low certainty.

text.text: Similar to the food vs. non-food contrast, heterogeneous implementations of hunger and satiety manipulations are likely to contribute to these inconsistencies.
Additional differences in participant populations, rating scales, and study design further limit direct comparisons.

One source of uncertainty also lies in the fact that researchers cannot be sure which underlying construct is being investigated by probing participants' experience through self-reported items of "liking" and "wanting".

Both visual and orthonasal food cues are in theory associated with the anticipatory, rather than the consummatory, phase of food reward, since they are predictive of a future eating experience (Berridge, 1996 (Berridge, , 2009)).
text.formatted: Both visual and orthonasal food cues are in theory associated with the anticipatory, rather than the consummatory, phase of food reward, since they are predictive of a future eating experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Berridge, 1996</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Berridge, , 2009))</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is very intuitive in the visual domain: when presented with the photograph of a pizza, participants likely evaluate the pizza itself, therefore judging the expected eating experience, rather than how pleasurable the visual composition of the picture is.
Food odours, however, may occupy a more ambiguous position: they could function both as predictive cues for food consumption and as hedonic sensory experiences in their own right.

Consequently, while visual food cues likely primarily capture expectations regarding the future eating experience, hedonic ratings of food odours may reflect multiple psychological processes simultaneously, including the directly experienced pleasantness of the odour itself, expected liking of the associated food, and the anticipated pleasure of eating it.

This ambiguity could partly arise from the unique organisation of the olfactory system: whereas orthonasal olfaction typically precedes consumption and therefore functions as an anticipatory cue, retronasal olfaction is particularly relevant to the consummatory experience itself (Small et al., 2008).
text.formatted: This ambiguity could partly arise from the unique organisation of the olfactory system: whereas orthonasal olfaction typically precedes consumption and therefore functions as an anticipatory cue, retronasal olfaction is particularly relevant to the consummatory experience itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Small et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Food odours may therefore occupy a position at the interface between anticipatory and consummatory reward that has no direct equivalent in the visual domain, and any direct comparison of the two modalities is likely compromised by this difference in self-reported scales.
Considering the complexity of odour perception, we propose that future studies distinguish more explicitly between these different aspects of reward by phrasing rating questions accordingly.
For example, one may separately assess the pleasantness of the presented odour, the expected pleasantness of the associated food, and the anticipated pleasure of consuming it.
In this context, Piacentini et al. (1993) asked their participants to rate the pleasantness of the imagined taste that was associated with the odour stimulus.

text.text: Such an approach may help standardise which aspect of the sensory experience participants are asked to evaluate, thereby improving comparability across studies.

text.text: Beyond comparing vision and olfaction, future work should also extend modality comparisons to other anticipatory sensory cues, including haptic information, and should systematically investigate both their independent and combined contributions to food reward.
Our synthesis of the reviewed literature is limited by inconsistency in categorisation of odours into food and non-food classes across the literature.
Some odours, such as coffee, were considered food stimuli in some studies but non-food in others.
Likewise, cultural differences may influence whether certain odours are perceived as edible (e.g., rose being strictly floral vs. evoking rose-water associations).

Furthermore, studies differed in the level of categorisation, with some contrasting food vs. non-food odours while others distinguished between more specific subclasses such as high-vs. low-energy or high-protein foods, thereby complicating direct comparisons across studies.

Furthermore, across the studies included in this review, 17 investigated exclusively one gender and one study did not report gender at all, substantially limiting the generalisability of the evidence.
Some authors justified this decision by citing reported sex differences in olfactory sensitivity (e.g., Albrecht et al., 2009).

text.text: Howeverhttps://sciwheel.com/work/citation?ids=8540350&pre=&suf=&sa=0&dbf=0 meta-analytic evidence shows that these differences are likely small (Sorokowski et al., 2019) , and their underlying causes may involve both biological and sociocultural factors.

text.text: Moreover, differences in olfactory sensitivity do not necessarily imply differences in reward processing, particularly when within-subject designs are used to investigate changes in reward as a function of metabolic state.

Unless a specific research question warrants restricting recruitment, future studies should aim to include more representative samples rather than assuming that one group is more appropriate for investigating food-related reward.

In addition to these literature-based limitations, we highlight that this review did not include a meta-analysis and, consequently, publication bias could not be formally assessed using methods such as funnel plots or regression-based approaches.
Nevertheless, we included a measure of publication bias using the GRADE framework.

Furthermore, many methodological tools developed for systematic reviews, including GRADE and several PRISMA recommendations, were originally designed for clinical intervention studies and meta-analytic approaches.
Their application to this review therefore required several adaptations.
While these adaptations were justified by the nature of the available literature, they inevitably limit the immediate transferability of our adapted measures to other reviews using the same systems.

The findings of this review suggest that food odours can elicit stronger reward responses than non-food odours, although this effect is not consistently observed and may depend on moderating factors, while comparisons with visual food cues provide no clear evidence of an advantage for either modality.
Given the limited certainty of the available evidence, further research is needed to establish whether food odours have distinct rewarding properties and under which conditions these emerge.
Given the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity in the literature, we propose recommendations for a structured approach for future studies in Table 4.

text.text: Clearly define the reward construct being investigated to distinguish the pleasantness associated with the experience of a sensory stimulus (i.e. odour), expected liking of the associated food (i.e. food associated with odour), and wanting to consume it.
Ratings should explicitly reflect the intended construct.
Planning
Systematically compare sensory modalities through the investigation food-associated cues across olfaction, vision and potentially other modalities, such as touch.
Where possible, use content-matched stimuli and assess both the independent and combined contributions of different modalities.
Planning
Broaden the diversity of experimental odour stimuli by moving beyond the set of frequently used odours identified in the (co)occurrence plot to determine whether findings generalise.
Planning

Select the experimental stimuli with purpose by exploring the odour space with the study's goal in mind: • for easily recognisable odours, commonly used odours can be selected • if replication is the goal, commonly used odours can be selected • if generalisation is the goal, less commonly used odours may be selected • some odours may better suited for comparing or contrast cultural influences on odour perception • when addressing the effects of metabolic states, taste associations of different odours should be considered Planning Metabolic states Improve the control of metabolic-state manipulations by Standardising or systematically varying fasting duration, meal composition and testing time.
Distinguish general satiety from sensory-specific satiety by considering the correspondence between consumed foods and tested odours.
Sampling Odour classification Use transparent criteria for classifying odours as food or non-food, recognising that food associations may vary across individuals and cultures.
Where appropriate, assess participants' own associations with the stimuli or select stimuli based on these associations.
Recruit more representative samples and avoid restricting recruitment by sex or gender without a clear scientific justification.
Instead, investigate potential group differences when theoretically relevant.
